speaker: Chris Urmson
title: The Road to Autonomy: Chris Urmson on Building Aurora
question: In commercial trucking, why do large freight fleets replace their semi-trucks roughly every three years?
guest: There are a couple of reasons that drive it. One is that these are very much total-cost-of-ownership businesses. Thoughtful trucking companies know that at that three-year point, maintenance costs go up and uptime goes down, so that's the time to rotate the truck out before it drops below their profitability targets. Another reason is that they're trying to hire new drivers. If you're a truck driver, one of the things that's appealing to you is getting a new truck rather than one that someone else drove for the last three years and slept in. And then, yes, they also drive a huge number of miles—today they average about 150,000 miles a year, which is roughly 10 to 15 times what you or I drive.

points.core: Fleets retire trucks right before rising maintenance costs erode uptime profitability targets.

Large fleets trade trucks on short cycles (typically three to five years, with the biggest truckload carriers at the short end) because it minimizes total cost of ownership rather than purchase cost.

A long-haul tractor runs 100,000 to 120,000 miles or more a year, so by year three or four it is approaching 400,000 to 500,000 miles. That is about when factory powertrain warranties expire and maintenance costs climb steeply: emissions aftertreatment systems, injectors, turbos, clutches and other expensive components start failing. Selling before that point shifts those repair costs and the associated downtime to the second owner.

Several other factors reinforce the timing. Resale values are still strong at that mileage, and large fleets often negotiate guaranteed trade-in or buyback terms with manufacturers. Newer trucks get better fuel economy, and fuel is one of a fleet's largest expenses. Breakdowns are costly in missed deliveries and towing, so reliability matters. Tax depreciation on tractors is front-loaded over about three years. Finally, new equipment with current safety and comfort features helps recruit and retain drivers in a high-turnover industry.

Large freight fleets replace their semi-trucks roughly every three years to minimize total cost of ownership by trading vehicles right before operating expenses spike. Long-haul tractors typically log 100,000 to 130,000 miles annually, reaching 300,000 to 400,000 miles around the three-year mark—precisely when comprehensive factory warranties expire and costly repairs to engines, transmissions, and emissions systems accelerate. Cycling trucks out at this inflection point prevents expensive roadside breakdowns, protects strict delivery schedules, and lets carriers run leaner in-house maintenance operations.

At the same time, three-year-old tractors still command strong resale value in the secondary market among smaller fleets and owner-operators, an economic sweet spot often reinforced by manufacturer buyback guarantees, full-service leases, and tax depreciation schedules. Frequent turnover also continuously upgrades the fleet with more aerodynamic, fuel-efficient trucks and modern collision-mitigation technology, lowering both diesel and insurance costs. Finally, putting drivers in late-model, reliable rigs with comfortable cabs helps large carriers recruit and retain talent in a high-turnover labor market.

noweb.answer:
Large freight fleets replace their semi-trucks roughly every three years—typically between 350,000 and 450,000 miles—because doing so minimizes their total cost per mile. That window aligns closely with the expiration of comprehensive factory warranties; once coverage ends, expensive repairs to complex emissions systems and drivetrains climb sharply, along with unscheduled roadside downtime that can jeopardize strict shipper contracts.

Trading tractors at this mileage also captures peak resale value on the secondary market, where smaller carriers and owner-operators actively seek late-model used trucks with plenty of remaining engine life. Because mega-fleets negotiate steep volume discounts with manufacturers and align financing and tax depreciation with a three-year trade cycle, refreshing equipment early is often cheaper than maintaining aging trucks in-house. Finally, upgrading continuously locks in steady gains in aerodynamics and fuel economy—yielding major savings across thousands of vehicles—while newer cab comforts and active safety systems lower insurance risk and help recruit and retain drivers in a high-turnover industry.

Large fleets replace semi-trucks every three or so years because that's usually when the total cost per mile is lowest. Long-haul trucks often run 100,000 to 150,000 miles a year, so three years means roughly 400,000 to 500,000 miles. Around that point the manufacturer's powertrain warranty typically ends, and costly repairs start to pile up: injectors, turbochargers, aftertreatment systems, clutches and eventually engine overhauls. Breakdowns also cause downtime, which costs fleets lost revenue and missed deliveries.

A lightly used truck also sells or trades in for a good price, so fleets get back much of their investment before depreciation and wear eat into it. Large fleets can buy new trucks at volume discounts, and depreciation write-offs give them a tax advantage. Each new generation of trucks tends to use somewhat less fuel and has better safety and emissions technology, and fuel is one of a fleet's biggest costs. Newer, more comfortable trucks also help recruit and keep drivers.

The interval isn't fixed. Many fleets keep trucks for four or five years, and smaller operators often run them much longer. Fleets also adjust timing depending on used-truck prices, interest rates and upcoming emissions rules.

Large freight fleets typically replace semi-trucks every three to four years—around 300,000 to 500,000 miles—to minimize total cost of ownership per mile. Around this mark, factory warranties on powertrains and complex emissions aftertreatment systems expire, and maintenance costs and unplanned downtime begin to climb steeply. For high-utilization carriers, a single breakdown means missed deliveries, expensive roadside repairs, and idle drivers.

Three years also hits a financial sweet spot. In the United States, over-the-road tractors qualify as three-year property under MACRS tax depreciation, letting fleets write off the trucks quickly, while trading them in at that age preserves strong resale value on the secondary market—often to smaller carriers or owner-operators willing to absorb higher maintenance in exchange for lower purchase prices. Finally, frequent turnover lets large fleets capture incremental gains in fuel efficiency and safety technology, lower insurance risk, and offer newer, more comfortable cabs that help recruit and retain drivers in a high-turnover industry.

noweb.answer:
Large freight fleets typically replace semi-trucks every three to four years—roughly 300,000 to 500,000 miles—to minimize total cost of ownership and maximize uptime. At that point, factory warranties on expensive components like powertrains and emissions systems begin to expire, and the risk of costly, unpredictable breakdowns rises sharply. For high-volume carriers, a single sidelined truck means missed deliveries, towing bills, and idle drivers, which quickly outweighs the cost of newer equipment.

Trading trucks in around year three also hits a financial sweet spot. The tractors still command strong resale value on the secondary market—where smaller fleets and owner-operators buy well-maintained used trucks—while aligning neatly with the three-year U.S. tax depreciation schedule for highway tractors. Finally, frequent cycling lets fleets continuously adopt better fuel efficiency, updated safety technology, and more comfortable cabs, lowering operating costs per mile and helping recruit and retain drivers.
